content: 1. The weight gain of infants should be monitored on a weekly basis to detect any changes. 2. If an infant fails to gain weight or loses weight despite the mother or caregiver receiving breastfeeding support, the infant should be referred to inpatient care for further evaluation and management. 3. The physical and mental health of mothers or caregivers should be assessed regularly, and appropriate treatment or support should be provided as necessary. This is a strong recommendation, although the supporting evidence is of very low quality. 4. Research priorities have been identified to address gaps in evidence related to the management of severe acute malnutrition in infants and children. These priorities span basic science, clinical care, epidemiology, and operational strategies. 5. Severe acute malnutrition in children aged 6–59 months is defined as a weight-for-height less than -3 Z-scores of the WHO growth standards median, or the presence of bilateral nutritional edema, or a mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) less than 115 mm. 6. Severe acute malnutrition is a significant global health issue, contributing to childhood morbidity, mortality, impaired intellectual development, reduced adult work capacity, and increased risk of diseases in adulthood. 7. It is estimated that 19 million preschool-aged children, primarily in the WHO African and South-East Asia regions, suffer from severe wasting. Severe wasting accounts for approximately 400,000 child deaths annually. 8. WHO growth standards for children aged 0–5 years, introduced in 2006, serve as the basis for defining and estimating malnutrition, including severe acute malnutrition. 9. Children with severe acute malnutrition have profoundly disturbed physiology and metabolism. Initiating intensive refeeding without correcting metabolic and electrolyte imbalances can result in high mortality rates. 10. Ready-to-use therapeutic foods (RUTFs) are increasingly used for outpatient treatment of uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition. These high-energy, fortified foods are safe for home use, do not require refrigeration, and are effective in treating malnutrition. 11. The management of severe acute malnutrition in children with HIV presents unique challenges. Optimal timing and dosing of antiretroviral therapy, as well as appropriate feeding regimens, require further research. 12. Severe acute malnutrition is increasingly documented in infants under 6 months of age, but there is limited data on their pathophysiology and the best therapeutic feeding approaches, including breastfeeding support. 13. WHO has commissioned systematic reviews and convened expert groups to develop guidelines for managing severe acute malnutrition in infants under 6 months of age. 14. The implications of the WHO child growth standards on populations defined as having severe acute malnutrition need further examination, particularly in different epidemiological settings. 15. Admission and discharge criteria for children aged 6–59 months with severe acute malnutrition require revision to ensure appropriate care transitions between inpatient and outpatient settings. 16. The use of antibiotics in outpatient management of severe acute malnutrition, the role of vitamin A supplementation, and the most effective therapeutic feeding approaches are areas requiring further evidence. 17. Fluid management strategies for children with severe acute malnutrition and dehydration, with or without shock, need to be optimized for safety and effectiveness. 18. The management of diarrhea in children with severe acute malnutrition, particularly in those receiving RUTFs, requires further investigation to ensure safety and efficacy. 19. The development of revised guidelines for managing severe acute malnutrition aims to address these gaps and improve outcomes for affected children globally.
